title: Aeneas apud Anium. Scylla
titleEn: Aeneas at Anius’ Court; the Cup of Alcon — Metamorphoses XIII.623–749
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Fate does not let hope fall with Troy: Aeneas carries the city’s sacred things and his father out on his shoulders, sails from Antandros past the Thracian shore where Polydorus’ blood is still in the ground, and comes to Apollo’s city, where the priest-king Anius receives him and tells how Agamemnon dragged four of his five children out of his lap by armed force and set them to feed the Greek fleet, and how Bacchus answered their prayer in a way Anius cannot explain and they went off as white doves. The oracle sends the Trojans to find their ancient mother; they read that as Crete, cannot bear the climate, and go on by the Strophades and Ulysses’ islands, see Ambracia and Dodona that speaks through its oak, put in at the Phaeacians’ orchards and at Buthrotos with its imitation Troy, and reach the three capes of Sicily, where the fleet grounds at nightfall on the sand of Zancle, Scylla infesting the one side and Charybdis the other. Anius’ parting gift, a mixing-bowl engraved with Thebes in mourning and the daughters of Orion dying for their people, is described at length; the part breaks off as Galatea, having her hair combed by Scylla, begins to say why she could escape the Cyclops’ love only through grief.

sentences.t:
Non tamen eversam Troiae cum moenibus esse
spem quoque fata sinunt:
sentences.l: Yet the fates do not allow hope too to have been overthrown together with the walls of Troy:
sentences.i: The fates, though, do not let hope go down with Troy’s walls as well:
sentences.n: The part opens on a refusal. sinunt, “they allow”, governs an accusative and infinitive, eversam ... esse spem, so what the fates will not allow is that hope should have been overthrown — a perfect passive infinitive, the thing done and finished. The phrase is split across the line-end: eversam stands in 623 and its noun spem opens 624, with Troiae cum moenibus esse between them. quoque is the plain adverb “too”, hung on spem, and not the quō-que, “and with which”, that the same four letters can be elsewhere. tamen, “yet”, turns the page on the sack of the city.

sentences.t:
sacra et, sacra altera, patrem
fert umeris, venerabile onus, Cythereius heros:
sentences.l: the sacred things, and — a second sacred thing — his father, the Cytherean hero carries on his shoulders, a burden to be revered:
sentences.i: the Cytherean hero carries the sacred images, and his father, a second sacred thing, on his shoulders — a burden worth reverence:
sentences.n: sacra is the neuter plural noun, the city’s holy objects; sacra altera is the same word again, in apposition to patrem, so the father is counted as a second set of holy things. venerabile onus is a further apposition to patrem. The subject is kept back to the very end of the sentence, and when it comes it is not a name: Cythereius heros, “the Cytherean hero”, identifies Aeneas by his mother Venus, whose island is Cythera — that is, by the parent he is not carrying. The edition joins the clause with a colon where English would write a semicolon, as it did at the end of the sentence before.

sentences.t:
de tantis opibus praedam pius eligit illam
Ascaniumque suum profugaque per aequora classe
fertur ab Antandro
sentences.l: out of such great wealth the dutiful man picks that plunder and his own Ascanius, and with his fleet in flight over the open sea he is carried from Antandros
sentences.i: out of all that wealth the dutiful son chooses that for his loot, and Ascanius with it, and is carried away from Antandros with his fleet in flight across the open sea
sentences.n: praedam ... illam stands in apposition to what he has just been said to carry: what a man takes out of a sacked city is loot, and the poem uses the word for loot of the gods and the father. pius, “dutiful”, stands where a name would and does a name’s work; the same adjective goes to Anchises at 640 and its noun, pietas, to the brother who fails at 663. profuga ... classe is an ablative with the two words held apart by per aequora. fertur is passive, “he is carried”: the man doing the carrying is himself carried. The sentence does not end here — it runs on through the next unit to the close of 631.

sentences.t:
scelerataque limina Thracum
et Polydoreo manantem sanguine terram
linquit et utilibus ventis aestuque secundo
intrat Apollineam sociis comitantibus urbem.
sentences.l: and the accursed thresholds of the Thracians and the earth running with Polydorean blood he leaves, and with useful winds and a following tide he enters, his companions accompanying him, the Apollonian city.
sentences.i: and he leaves behind the Thracians’ accursed doorway and the ground still running with Polydorus’ blood, and with a helping wind and the tide behind him he comes into Apollo’s city, his companions with him.
sentences.n: The verb linquit is held back to the head of 630 and governs two objects reached back over three lines, limina and terram. Polydoreo ... sanguine is an adjective made out of a personal name, which Latin does easily and English can only manage with a genitive. In scelerata limina the crime is the host’s and the adjective is transferred to his doorway. sociis comitantibus is an ablative absolute — noun and participle standing free of the sentence’s grammar, where English wants a clause, “with his companions accompanying him” — and it is the first of many in this part. The city is Apollo’s and is never named in these lines: it is identified by the adjective Apollineam, by the priest-king of the next sentence, and at 650 by the god’s own title Delius, “the Delian”. aestu secundo, “with a following tide”, comes back word for word at 728, at the end of the voyage this line begins.

sentences.t:
Hunc Anius, quo rege homines, antistite Phoebus
rite colebatur, temploque domoque recepit
urbemque ostendit delubraque nota duasque
Latona quondam stirpes pariente retentas.
sentences.l: Him Anius, under whom as king men, as priest Phoebus, was duly tended, received in temple and in house, and showed him the city and the well-known shrines and the two trunks once held on to, with Latona giving birth.
sentences.i: Anius took him in, in the temple and in his house — Anius under whom as king men were cared for and as priest Phoebus was worshipped — and showed him the city, the famous shrines, and the two trunks Latona once held on to as she gave birth.
sentences.n: Two ablative absolutes share one verb: quo rege, “with him as king”, and antistite, “with him as priest”, the second a bare noun with the pronoun understood. colebatur is singular because it has gone to the nearer subject, Phoebus, and it has to be taken twice over in two senses, since colere is “tend, look after” of men and “worship” of a god — one Latin verb doing a double job English cannot make one verb do. temploque domoque, with -que on both, is the epic way of writing “both ... and”. duasque closes 634 and its noun stirpes stands third in 635, inside the ablative absolute Latona ... pariente that wraps around it. retentas is a perfect passive participle agreeing with stirpes and it names no agent: the Latin says the trunks were held on to, with Latona giving birth, and it is English that has to make her the one doing the holding. What the two trunks were is not said.

sentences.t:
Ture dato flammis vinoque in tura profuso
caesarumque boum fibris de more crematis
regia tecta petunt positisque tapetibus altis
munera cum liquido capiunt Cerealia Baccho.
sentences.l: Incense having been given to the flames and wine having been poured out over the incense, and the entrails of slaughtered oxen having been burned according to custom, they make for the royal roofs, and with deep coverlets laid out they take the gifts of Ceres with liquid Bacchus.
sentences.i: Once incense had been given to the flames, and wine poured out over the incense, and the entrails of the slaughtered oxen burned as custom requires, they make for the palace, and on the deep coverlets laid out for them they take Ceres’ gifts and Bacchus in liquid form.
sentences.n: Four ablative absolutes carry the ritual — ture dato, vino profuso, fibris crematis, and then positis tapetibus. The first three set the sacrifice down as finished before any main verb arrives; the fourth comes after petunt, in the second half of 638. Latin stacks them and English has to turn each one into a clause. petunt and capiunt are historic presents. The last line is two metonymies interlocked: munera ... Cerealia is bread, liquidus Bacchus is wine, each god’s name standing for the god’s gift, and liquido is needed because Bacchus by himself would be the god. The words are set munera, cum liquido, capiunt, Cerealia, Baccho, so that each noun is parted from its own adjective by the other pair and by the verb.

sentences.t:
Tum pius Anchises: “O Phoebi lecte sacerdos,
fallor, an et natum, cum primum haec moenia vidi,
bisque duas natas, quantum reminiscor, habebas?”
sentences.l: Then dutiful Anchises: “O chosen priest of Phoebus, am I deceived, or did you have both a son, when first I saw these walls, and twice two daughters, as far as I recall?”
sentences.i: Then Anchises, dutiful as ever: “Chosen priest of Phoebus — am I wrong, or when I first saw these walls did you have a son, and four daughters, as far as I remember?”
sentences.n: There is no verb of speaking: Tum pius Anchises stands with a colon after it, and the colon is the whole of “said”. fallor, an ...? is the ordinary polite Latin opening — a two-limbed question whose first limb offers the speaker’s own error before the question is asked. lecte is the perfect passive participle of lego, “chosen”, in the vocative. bis duas is “twice two”, four arrived at by multiplication, which verse prefers to a flat quattuor. Two comma-set asides, cum primum haec moenia vidi and quantum reminiscor, hedge the memory at both ends.

sentences.t:
Huic Anius niveis circumdata tempora vittis
concutiens et tristis ait:
sentences.l: To him Anius, shaking his temples encircled with snowy fillets, and sorrowful, says:
sentences.i: Anius answers him, shaking the temples his snow-white fillets bound, and sad as he speaks:
sentences.n: tempora is the direct object of the participle concutiens, “shaking”, and circumdata is a perfect passive participle agreeing with tempora, with vittis the ablative of what they are encircled by. The four words stand niveis circumdata tempora vittis, adjective and its noun at the two ends and the participle with its own noun inside them. vittae are the woollen bands of a priest’s office; their whiteness comes back at 674 on the birds his daughters become. tristis is a nominative adjective doing adverbial work, “sad” where English says “sadly”. Huic is the dative that ait takes.

sentences.t:
“Non falleris, heros
maxime: vidisti natorum quinque parentem,
quem nunc (tanta homines rerum inconstantia versat!)
paene vides orbum.
sentences.l: “You are not mistaken, greatest hero: you saw the parent of five children, whom now (such great inconstancy of things spins men about!) you see almost childless.
sentences.i: “You are not mistaken, greatest of heroes: you saw a father of five, and now — such is the fickleness of things that keeps men spinning! — you see him all but childless.
sentences.n: falleris is the passive of fallo used for “you are mistaken”, and it answers Anchises’ own fallor at 641 with the same verb, turned from first person to second. nati covers children of either sex and parens is a parent of either sex, so the count of five is made in words that specify nothing. The exclamation in round brackets is the edition’s own punctuation and it is dropped inside the relative clause, between quem nunc and paene vides orbum; versat is the verb of spinning a thing about, with inconstantia rerum as what does the spinning. orbus is the word for a parent bereft of children, predicative with vides — “you see him bereft” — and paene, “almost”, is there because one child is left.

sentences.t:
Quod enim mihi filius absens
auxilium, quem dicta suo de nomine tellus
Andros habet pro patre locumque et regna tenentem?
sentences.l: For what help to me is a son who is absent, whom the land called Andros from his own name has in a father’s place, holding the place and the realms?
sentences.i: For what good to me is a son who is not here, whom the land named Andros after him keeps in a father’s stead, holding the country and the throne?
sentences.n: est is left out, as Latin leaves it out in a question of this shape, and mihi is the dative of the person concerned: “what help is there for me”. dicta suo de nomine agrees with tellus, and Andros is a Greek nominative in apposition to it — the island wears the son’s name. pro patre can be taken two ways and both are alive: the island has him instead of the father he should be with, and it has him as a father, in a father’s place. regna is a poetic plural for one kingdom. tenentem is a present participle agreeing with quem, so the son is held by the island in the act of holding it.

sentences.t:
Delius augurium dedit huic, dedit altera Liber
femineae stirpi voto maiora fideque
munera:
sentences.l: The Delian gave prophecy to him; to the female stock Liber gave other gifts, greater than a prayer and than belief:
sentences.i: Apollo of Delos gave him prophecy; to the daughters Bacchus gave gifts of another kind, beyond praying for and beyond believing:
sentences.n: Neither god is called by the name a reader expects: Delius, “the Delian”, for Apollo, on the island the scene is set on, and Liber for Bacchus, who is Bacche in the daughters’ own prayer at 669. dedit ... dedit repeats the verb across the two halves of the line, the second time at the head of its own clause, and the second gift gets the longer half. altera is separated from its noun munera by the whole of 651: altera stands next to last in 650, before Liber, and munera opens 652. voto and fide are ablatives of comparison after maiora — greater than a vow, greater than credence, that is, beyond what a man would pray for or believe. femineae stirpi, “the female stock”, is a collective for the four daughters, as natorum at 645 was for all five children.

sentences.t:
nam tactu natarum cuncta mearum
in segetem laticemque meri canaeque Minervae
transformabantur, divesque erat usus in illis.
sentences.l: for by the touch of my daughters all things were being transformed into grain and into the liquid of unmixed wine and of grey Minerva, and rich was the use in them.
sentences.i: for at my daughters’ touch everything kept turning into corn, into the liquid of neat wine and of grey Minerva’s olive, and there was wealth in the using of them.
sentences.n: One noun, laticem, carries two genitives, meri and canae Minervae, so the single word “liquid” has to serve for the wine and for the oil. Minerva stands for her olive by metonymy, and cana, “grey-white”, is the colour of the oil and not of the goddess. With seges, the standing crop, the three gifts are corn, wine and oil — the three staples, each named by a figure instead of by its plain noun. transformabantur is imperfect passive, the tense of a thing that kept on happening. divesque erat usus in illis puts it flatly: what was rich was the use of them, and the daughters are described as an income in the line before Agamemnon hears of them.

sentences.t:
Hoc ubi cognovit Troiae populator Atrides,
ne non ex aliqua vestram sensisse procellam
nos quoque parte putes,
sentences.l: When the ravager of Troy, the son of Atreus, learned this — so that you may not think that we too have failed to feel your storm in some quarter —
sentences.i: When the man who laid Troy waste, Atreus’ son, heard of it — and you are not to think we too got off without feeling your storm from some quarter —
sentences.n: The ne-clause is a purpose clause belonging to Anius’ own act of telling and not to Agamemnon’s learning: he breaks off his sentence to say why he is telling the story at all. ne non is a double negative, “lest ... not”, and putes takes an accusative and infinitive, nos ... sensisse. vestram, “your”, makes the Trojan war the guests’ own storm, said to their faces without reproach. The preposition and its noun are split across the line-end: ex aliqua stands in the middle of 656, parte third in 657, with vestram sensisse procellam and nos quoque between them. populator, “ravager”, is Anius’ word for Agamemnon, spoken to the men whose city he ravaged. Atrides is a Greek patronymic. The sentence runs on into the next unit and ends at 659.

sentences.t:
armorum viribus usus
abstrahit invitas gremio genitoris, alantque
imperat Argolicam caelesti munere classem.
sentences.l: having used the strength of arms he drags them away unwilling from their father’s lap, and orders that they feed the Argive fleet by a gift of heaven.
sentences.i: he used armed force to drag them off, unwilling, out of their father’s lap, and ordered them to feed the Argive fleet with the gift heaven had given them.
sentences.n: usus is the perfect participle of the deponent utor and is active in meaning, “having used”, with the ablative armorum viribus that utor governs. invitas is a bare feminine accusative plural with no noun at all: the daughters are carried by the adjective alone, and what the adjective says about them is that they did not consent. gremio genitoris is an ablative of separation with no preposition, and genitor, “father”, is the speaker himself — Anius tells his own loss in the third person. alant is a subjunctive after imperat with no ut between them, the older parataxis. The verbs go into the historic present at the crisis, abstrahit and imperat, cutting into a story Anius has been telling in perfect and imperfect — dedit, transformabantur, erat, cognovit.

sentences.t:
Effugiunt, quo quaeque potest: Euboea duabus,
et totidem natis Andros fraterna petita est.
sentences.l: They flee, each one where she can: Euboea was sought by two, and by as many daughters brotherly Andros.
sentences.i: They scatter, each where she can: two of them made for Euboea, and as many for Andros, their brother’s island.
sentences.n: quaeque is distributive, “each in her own case”, with the singular verb potest; quo is “to where”. duabus and totidem natis are datives of the person by whom, taken with the perfect passive petita est — a dative of agent, which Latin normally allows only with the -ndus verbal adjective and which verse extends to this. fraterna, “brotherly”, does the work of a genitive: the island of 649 that carries the brother’s name is here an adjective. Effugiunt is a historic present and petita est a perfect, in one breath.

sentences.t: Miles adest et, ni dedantur, bella minatur.
sentences.l: The soldiery is at hand and, unless they are given up, threatens wars.
sentences.i: The troops are there, and they threaten war unless the daughters are handed over.
sentences.n: miles is a collective singular, one soldier standing for a whole army, which is standard in verse and has no short English equivalent. dedantur is a present subjunctive inside the threat: the condition is put as the man making it puts it, not as a fact of the narrative. bella is a poetic plural. The verb dedo comes back at the head of 664 in dedidit, so the thing demanded and the thing done are the same word.

sentences.t: Victa metu pietas:
sentences.l: Piety was conquered by fear:
sentences.i: Duty to his own was beaten by fear:
sentences.n: A participle, an ablative and a noun, with est left out — three words and a colon, as short as any sentence in this part — and it states the defeat before anything has been done. pietas is the noun of the adjective pius that this part has given to Aeneas at 626 and to Anchises at 640, so the virtue that carried a father out of Troy is the one that gives way here. metu is ablative, the fear by which it was beaten.

sentences.t:
consortia corpora poenae
dedidit (et timido possis ignoscere fratri:
sentences.l: he gave up the bodies that shared the penalty (and you could forgive a frightened brother:
sentences.i: he surrendered the bodies that were partners in the penalty (and one could forgive a frightened brother:
sentences.n: consors takes a genitive, so consortia ... poenae is “sharing in the penalty”, and the two words wrap around corpora at the end of 663: the sisters are named by their bodies and by the share of punishment those bodies stand for, not as sisters. The verb dedidit opens 664 and has no expressed subject at all — who did it is only settled by the parenthesis that follows, timido ... fratri. The round brackets are the edition’s own and what they open runs to the semicolon at the end of 666. possis is a potential subjunctive with the indefinite second person, “one could forgive”, though the man addressed is Anchises. ignoscere takes the dative. The brother is the absent son of 648, the one the daughters fled to at 661.

sentences.t:
non hic Aeneas, non, qui defenderet Andron,
Hector erat, per quem decimum durastis in annum);
sentences.l: here there was no Aeneas, no Hector, one to defend Andros, through whom you held out into the tenth year);
sentences.i: there was no Aeneas there, and no Hector to defend Andros — the man you held out through into the tenth year);
sentences.n: non ... non is anaphora, and the two names are given as types rather than as persons: a defender of the kind those two were. The relative clause of purpose qui defenderet, with its subjunctive — “one who might defend” — is pushed in between the second non and its noun, so Hector arrives only at the head of 666. Andron is the Greek accusative of Andros. durastis is syncopated duravistis, and it is second person plural, addressed to the Trojans at the table: the compliment to Hector is paid to Hector’s own people, by the priest whose own children the other side took.

sentences.t: iamque parabantur captivis vincla lacertis:
sentences.l: and now bonds were being made ready for the captive arms:
sentences.i: and now the chains were being got ready for their arms as prisoners:
sentences.n: parabantur is imperfect passive, the tense of an action under way and about to be cut off. captivis lacertis is a dative of the thing for which. The adjective is transferred — the arms are not captive, the women are — and the poem has now named the sisters twice by the body instead of by a name: corpora at 663, and here lacerti, the upper arms — the part a rope actually goes round.

sentences.t:
illae tollentes etiamnum libera caelo
bracchia “Bacche pater, fer opem!” dixere, tulitque
muneris auctor opem, —
sentences.l: they, raising to the sky arms still free, said “Father Bacchus, bring help!” and the giver of the gift brought help —
sentences.i: they lifted arms that were still free towards the sky and cried “Father Bacchus, bring help!” — and the author of the gift brought help —
sentences.n: dixere is dixerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere; there is no difference of meaning, only of metre and register, and this part uses the form again and again from here on. etiamnum libera, “still free”, is the whole force of the line: the chains of 667 are being made and are not yet on. bracchia is held back to the head of 669, a line away from the adjective libera that describes it. caelo is a dative of the direction of motion, which verse uses where prose would write ad caelum. muneris auctor names Bacchus by the gift of 650 to 654, and the answer comes back in the words of the prayer: fer opem, then tulit ... opem. The dash is the edition’s.

sentences.l: if destroying in a strange fashion is called bringing help, and by what means they lost their shape I could not learn, nor can I say now;
sentences.i: if to destroy someone in so strange a way counts as bringing help — and how they lost their shape I never could find out, and cannot tell you now;
sentences.n: The si-clause has its apodosis behind it rather than in front of it: it looks back to tulit ... opem, the statement it has just interrupted, and takes it back as it goes — he brought help, if destroying in a strange fashion is called bringing help. Nothing is added after the condition, and what Bacchus brought destroyed them. vocatur is passive, “is called”. perdiderint is a perfect subjunctive in an indirect question opened by qua ratione, and the whole question stands in front of the two verbs that govern it, potui scire and dicere possum, one past and one present, so the ignorance is stated twice over. Here a speaker says plainly that he does not know how a metamorphosis happened.

sentences.t: summa mali nota est:
sentences.l: the sum of the evil is known:
sentences.i: the total of the disaster is known:
sentences.n: summa is the accountant’s word for a total and mali is the genitive of the thing totted up: the bottom line of the harm. It answers the unit before it exactly — he does not know the manner, he knows the amount.

sentences.t:
pennas sumpsere tuaeque
coniugis in volucres, niveas abiere columbas.”
sentences.l: they took on feathers and went off into your wife’s birds, into snow-white doves.”
sentences.i: they took feathers, and passed into your wife’s birds, into snow-white doves.”
sentences.n: sumpsere and abiere are two more -ere perfects in a single sentence. in with the accusative is the regular way of naming what a shape passes into, and the two accusatives are in apposition, the general word first and the species after: birds, then doves. tuae coniugis is spoken to Anchises, whose consort was Venus, so these are the birds of Aeneas’ mother — the goddess who stood behind Cythereius heros at 625. niveas is the adjective of the priest’s own fillets at 643, and the speech ends on the snow-white birds.

sentences.t:
Talibus atque aliis postquam convivia dictis
implerunt, mensa somnum petiere remota,
cumque die surgunt adeuntque oracula Phoebi:
sentences.l: After they had filled the feast with such words and others, with the table taken away they sought sleep, and they rise with the day and go to the oracles of Phoebus:
sentences.i: When they had filled the evening with talk of that kind and more, the table was taken away and they went looking for sleep; and they rise with the day and go to Phoebus’ oracle:
sentences.n: postquam is the fourth word of its own clause, after Talibus atque aliis — Latin puts its conjunctions where it likes and English cannot. It takes a plain perfect indicative, implerunt. mensa ... remota is an ablative absolute wrapped round somnum petiere, so the clearing of the table encloses the going to bed. petiere is another -ere perfect. Then the tense changes: implerunt and petiere are perfect, surgunt and adeunt historic present, and the new day begins in the livelier tense. cum die is “as the day came up”.

sentences.t:
qui petere antiquam matrem cognataque iussit
litora;
sentences.l: and he ordered them to seek their ancient mother and the shores of their kin;
sentences.i: and he told them to make for their ancient mother and the coasts they were related to;
sentences.n: qui opens the sentence and is a connecting relative — “and he”, not “who”: Latin starts a new sentence with the relative pronoun where English starts it with a pronoun. This is the first of four in the part. iussit takes a bare infinitive, petere, and leaves the persons ordered unexpressed. antiqua mater is the oracle’s riddle and it is not explained here; the reading they put on it is at 705 to 707, where they take it for Crete and cannot stay. cognata litora makes a coastline a blood relation.

sentences.t:
prosequitur rex et dat munus ituris,
Anchisae sceptrum, chlamydem pharetramque nepoti,
cratera Aeneae, quem quondam transtulit illi
hospes ab Aoniis Therses Ismenius oris.
sentences.l: the king escorts them and gives a gift to those about to go: to Anchises a sceptre, to the grandson a cloak and a quiver, to Aeneas a mixing-bowl, which once Therses of Ismenus, a guest-friend, brought over to him from the Aonian shores.
sentences.i: the king walks them down and gives each of them a parting present: a sceptre for Anchises, a cloak and a quiver for the grandson, a mixing-bowl for Aeneas — one that Therses of Ismenus, a guest-friend, had brought him long ago from the shores of Aonia.
sentences.n: ituris is the future participle of eo in the dative plural — one word for “to them as they were about to go”. The three gifts are laid out without connectives, each recipient in the dative, and the boy named as Ascanius at 627 is here only nepoti, “the grandson”, placed by his relation to the two men beside him. cratera is a Greek accusative singular. hospes is the guest-friend, the standing bond that makes the gift possible: Therses gave it to Anius as Anius now gives it on. Ismenius is from the Theban river Ismenos and Aoniis is Boeotian, so the cup comes from Thebes — which is what the scene engraved on it turns out to be at 692.

sentences.t:
Miserat hunc illi Therses, fabricaverat Alcon
Hyleus et longo caelaverat argumento.
sentences.l: Therses had sent this to him; Alcon of Hyle had made it and had engraved it with a long story.
sentences.i: Therses had sent it to him; Alcon of Hyle had made it and worked it over with a long scene.
sentences.n: Three pluperfects run the cup backwards in time behind the giving of 681 — sent, then made, then engraved. The first two clauses are set side by side with nothing between them and the third is joined on by et, so only the last join is made. Demonstratives do the work of names, hunc for the bowl and illi for Anius. caelare is to work metal in relief, and argumentum is the subject-matter of a picture, so longo argumento is an ablative of means, “with a long story on it”. Hyleus places Alcon at Hyle, and the cup is the one object given in these lines whose maker is named at all.

sentences.t: Urbs erat, et septem posses ostendere portas:
sentences.l: There was a city, and you could point out seven gates:
sentences.i: There was a city, and you could have pointed out seven gates:
sentences.n: erat is the imperfect of description, the tense a picture is set out in. posses is a potential subjunctive in past time with the indefinite second person — “one could” — which is the standard Latin way of describing a work of art: the reader is stood in front of it and invited to look. The seven gates identify the city without naming it, and the name does not come until 692.

sentences.t: hae pro nomine erant et, quae foret illa, docebant.
sentences.l: these stood in place of a name and taught which one it was.
sentences.i: they served instead of a name, and told you which city it was.
sentences.n: quae foret illa is an indirect question after docebant, and foret is the alternative imperfect subjunctive of sum, which verse uses freely for esset. pro nomine makes the gates the caption of the picture: the relief carries no lettering, so the number is the label — and docebant credits the gates themselves with the teaching.

sentences.t:
Ante urbem exequiae tumulique ignesque rogique
effusaeque comas et apertae pectora matres
significant luctum:
sentences.l: Before the city, funeral processions and burial-mounds and fires and pyres, and mothers loosened as to their hair and open as to their breasts, signify mourning:
sentences.i: In front of the city: funeral processions, grave-mounds, fires, pyres, and mothers with their hair let loose and their breasts laid bare — all of it signifies mourning:
sentences.n: comas with effusae and pectora with apertae are Greek accusatives of respect: both participles are passive in form, and the accusative names the part of the body each holds of — “loosened as to the hair”, “laid open as to the breast”. It is a Greek turn taken into Latin verse, and this part uses it again at 732. -que three times in 687, and again on effusae at the head of 688, piles the funeral furniture up without ranking any of it. significant is present tense: a relief is described as doing now what it shows.

sentences.t:
nymphae quoque flere videntur
siccatosque queri fontes, sine frondibus arbor
nuda riget, rodunt arentia saxa capellae.
sentences.l: the nymphs too seem to weep and to complain of their springs dried up, a tree without leaves stands stiff and bare, she-goats gnaw the parched rocks.
sentences.i: the nymphs too seem to be weeping and complaining that their springs are dried up; a bare tree stands stiff and leafless; the she-goats gnaw at parched stones.
sentences.n: quoque is the plain adverb, “too”. videntur, “they seem”, is the honest verb for a picture: worked bronze can only show what looks like weeping, and the poem says so rather than pretending otherwise. queri is deponent and active in meaning, with siccatos ... fontes as its object. The close drops every connective and gives the drought in two flat clauses, the tree and the goats, with riget — the verb of stiffness, of ice and of things that will not bend — used of a bare tree.

sentences.t:
Ecce facit mediis natas Orione Thebis,
agmen femineum, iugulo dare pectus aperto,
sentences.l: Look — he makes the daughters born of Orion, a column of women, in the middle of Thebes offer their breast with the throat laid open,
sentences.i: And look: he shows Orion’s daughters, a column of women, in the middle of Thebes, giving their breast to the blade with their throats laid open,
sentences.n: facit is the artist’s verb, “he makes them do it”, and it governs everything down to 699 through a string of infinitives: dare here, then cecidisse, ferri, cremari, exire and ducere. Orione is an ablative of origin with no preposition, “born of Orion”, the same construction as at 717 and 749. mediis ... Thebis is a bare ablative of place, and it names at last the city the seven gates stood for at 685. agmen is a military word, a column on the march, and femineum is added because the word is strange where it stands. iugulo ... aperto is an ablative absolute. The sentence runs on through the next two units.

sentences.t:
illas demisso per inertia vulnera telo
pro populo cecidisse suo pulchrisque per urbem
funeribus ferri celebrique in parte cremari,
sentences.l: that they fell for their own people, with the weapon lowered through wounds that did not fight back, and are carried through the city in beautiful funerals and burned in a crowded quarter,
sentences.i: that they fell for their own people, the blade driven down through wounds that put up no resistance, and are carried through the city in splendid funerals and burned in a crowded quarter,
sentences.n: The tenses of the infinitives are exact: cecidisse is perfect, the dying already over, while ferri and cremari are present passives, the carrying and the burning still going on — a relief shows all three at once and the grammar keeps them apart. demisso ... telo is an ablative absolute. inertia is the hard word, “without force, doing nothing”, transferred from the women to their wounds, so that what fails to resist is the wound itself. pro populo ... suo is split around cecidisse. Magnus prints demisso per inertia vulnera telo; some editions print illac ... per fortia pectora, “through brave breasts”, which turns the unresisting wound into a courageous body and reverses the point.

sentences.t:
tum de virginea geminos exire favilla,
ne genus intereat, iuvenes, quos fama Coronos
nominat, et cineri materno ducere pompam.
sentences.l: then that twins come out of the maiden ash, so that the race should not die out — young men whom report names the Coroni — and lead the procession for their mother’s ashes.
sentences.i: then that twins come out of the girls’ ashes, so the line should not die out — young men whom report calls the Coroni — and walk at the head of the procession for their mother’s ash.
sentences.n: geminos stands fourth in 697 and its noun iuvenes arrives only in 698, after the purpose clause ne genus intereat has been let in between them. virginea favilla transfers the adjective from the girls to the ash they have become. cineri materno is a dative, “for their mother’s ash”, and materno is deliberate and strange: the twins come out of the ashes of girls who are mothers only by having produced them. Magnus prints Coronos, a Greek accusative plural agreeing with quos and iuvenes; some editions print Coronas. The sentence that began at 692 ends with this unit, having run from 692 to 699 as a single accusative and infinitive.

sentences.t:
Hactenus antiquo signis fulgentibus aere,
summus inaurato crater erat asper acantho.
sentences.l: So far in ancient bronze, with the figures shining; the topmost bowl was rough with gilded acanthus.
sentences.i: So much for the old bronze and the figures standing out bright on it; the rim of the bowl was rough with gilded acanthus.
sentences.n: hactenus, “up to this point”, closes the description, and its clause has no verb at all: both ablatives, antiquo ... aere and signis fulgentibus, hang on a verb the reader has to supply out of the sentences before. summus crater is “the topmost part of the bowl”, the idiom by which summus mons is the top of the mountain and not a high mountain. asper is the technical word for relief-work — rough, because the ornament stands up off the surface. The bronze is ancient and the acanthus is gilded, so the last thing said of the cup is the difference between the two.

sentences.t:
Nec leviora datis Troiani dona remittunt
dantque sacerdoti custodem turis acerram,
dant pateram claramque auro gemmisque coronam.
sentences.l: And the Trojans send back gifts not lighter than those given, and they give the priest a casket, the guardian of his incense, they give a bowl and a crown bright with gold and gems.
sentences.i: The Trojans send back gifts no slighter than the ones they were given: they give the priest an incense-box to keep his incense in, a libation-bowl, and a crown bright with gold and jewels.
sentences.n: nec leviora is litotes: “not lighter” means “fully as heavy”, and it lets the Trojans be generous without any boasting in the sentence. datis is a perfect passive participle used as a noun in the ablative of comparison, “than the things given”. custodem is in apposition to acerram, so the incense-box is given an office and a title, “the guardian of the incense”. dant ... dant is anaphora, the first joined on with -que and the second left with no connective at all.

sentences.t:
Inde recordati Teucros a sanguine Teucri
ducere principium, Cretam tenuere locique
ferre diu nequiere Iovem, centumque relictis
urbibus Ausonios optant contingere portus:
sentences.l: Then, remembering that the Teucrians drew their beginning from the blood of Teucer, they held for Crete and could not long bear the Jupiter of the place, and with a hundred cities left behind they long to reach the harbours of Ausonia:
sentences.i: Then, remembering that the Teucrians took their origin from Teucer’s blood, they made for Crete — and could not long stand the climate there, and, with a hundred cities left behind them, set their hearts on reaching the harbours of Ausonia:
sentences.n: recordati is the perfect participle of a deponent and is active in meaning, “having remembered”; it governs the accusative and infinitive Teucros ... ducere principium. This is the reading they give the oracle’s antiqua mater of 678, and it fails at once. locique ... Iovem is metonymy of the plainest kind, the sky-god for the sky, so what they cannot bear is the weather. tenuere and nequiere are -ere perfects. centum ... urbibus with relictis is an ablative absolute, with the number held back from its noun across the line-end. optant is a historic present after two perfects, and it is the verb of wanting a thing, not of getting it.

sentences.t:
saevit hiems iactatque viros, Strophadumque receptos
portubus infidis exterruit ales Aello.
sentences.l: a storm rages and tosses the men about, and the winged Aello terrified them, taken as they were into the treacherous harbours of the Strophades.
sentences.i: a storm rages and flings the men about; and once the treacherous harbours of the Strophades had taken them in, Aello the winged one terrified them.
sentences.n: hiems here is the storm, not the season. saevit and iactat are historic present and exterruit is perfect in one sentence, so the storm goes on while the fright is over and done with: this alternation is how the narrative changes speed. receptos is a perfect passive participle in the accusative with no noun of its own, doing the work of a clause about the men. infidis, “not to be trusted”, is the point of the harbour: it takes them in and then holds them. ales is “the winged one”, and Aello is a Greek name meaning storm-blast, so the storm of the line before comes back in the shape of a bird.

sentences.t:
Et iam Dulichios portus Ithacamque Samonque
Neritiasque domus, regnum fallacis Ulixis,
praeter erant vecti:
sentences.l: And by now they had been carried past the Dulichian harbours and Ithaca and Samos and the Neritian houses, the kingdom of lying Ulysses:
sentences.i: And by now they had sailed past the harbours of Dulichium, Ithaca, Samos and the houses of Neritos — the kingdom of the liar Ulysses:
sentences.n: The compound verb praetervehor is pulled apart: praeter stands at the head of 713 and the auxiliary is put between it and its own participle, praeter erant vecti, so the whole list of places sits inside the verb that goes past them. Samon is a Greek accusative. fallax is “deceiving, treacherous”, and the poem hangs it on Ulysses’ name here; both layers keep the insult at its strength rather than softening it to “clever”. regnum ... Ulixis stands in apposition to everything listed before it, so four place-names turn out to be one man’s kingdom.

sentences.t:
certatam lite deorum
Ambraciam versique vident sub imagine saxum
iudicis, Actiaco quae nunc ab Apolline nota est,
sentences.l: they see Ambracia, contested in a lawsuit of the gods, and a rock under the likeness of the judge who was turned, which is now known from Actian Apollo,
sentences.i: they see Ambracia, which the gods went to law over, and a rock that keeps the shape of the judge who was turned to stone — the place now famous for Apollo of Actium —
sentences.n: certatam is a perfect passive participle of certo, a verb that normally has neither passive nor object; here it has both, and lite deorum is the ablative of the quarrel it was contested in, lis being the word for a lawsuit. versi ... iudicis is a genitive with imagine — the judge who decided the gods’ case and was turned to stone for it, told in two words and never named in these lines. quae is feminine singular, so it reaches back over the neuter saxum standing next to it to Ambraciam: the relative agrees with the further noun, not the nearer. nunc measures from the poet’s own day, not from the voyage. The sentence runs on to the end of 718.

sentences.t:
vocalemque sua terram Dodonida quercu
Chaoniosque sinus, ubi nati rege Molosso
inpia subiectis fugere incendia pennis.
sentences.l: and the Dodonian land, speaking by its own oak, and the Chaonian bays, where sons born of the Molossian king escaped unholy fires on wings put beneath them.
sentences.i: and Dodona’s land, that speaks through its own oak, and the bays of Chaonia, where the sons of the Molossian king escaped an unholy burning on wings put beneath them.
sentences.n: vocalem, “having a voice”, is given to the land, while the thing that actually speaks stands in the ablative — sua ... quercu, “by its own oak”. Dodonida is a Greek feminine accusative. nati rege Molosso is another ablative of origin with no preposition, as at 692 and 749. subiectis ... pennis is an ablative of means with a participle inside it — “with wings put beneath them” — and not an absolute: pennis is the thing they escaped by, so it belongs to fugere and cannot stand free of it. fugere is fugerunt, an -ere perfect. And the edition’s spelling is worth seeing: inpia keeps n before p, where the same edition prints impune at 741 and impediere at 745. Magnus does not level these forms and Lectorium prints what he prints.

sentences.t:
Proxima Phaeacum felicibus obsita pomis
rura petunt, Epiros ab his regnataque vati
Buthrotos Phrygio simulataque Troia tenetur.
sentences.l: Next they seek the fields of the Phaeacians, planted thick with fruitful apples; after these, Epirus is held for, and Buthrotos, ruled by a Phrygian seer, and a Troy made in imitation.
sentences.i: Next they make for the Phaeacians’ countryside, thick-planted with trees in fruit; after that they hold their course for Epirus, and for Buthrotos under its Phrygian prophet, and the Troy built there in imitation.
sentences.n: Proxima is split from its noun across the line-end: it opens 719, and rura opens 720, with four words of description between them. felix of a tree is the farmer’s word for fruit-bearing, and obsita is “sown over, planted thick”. tenetur is one passive verb serving three subjects, Epiros, Buthrotos and Troia, agreeing with the nearest of them; teneo of holding a course for a place is the same use as Cretam tenuere at 706. regnata takes a dative of the agent, vati ... Phrygio — regno is intransitive in prose and the passive participle is a poetic stretch — and the two words of that phrase stand on either side of Buthrotos, vati closing 720 and Phrygio second in 721. The seer is not named in this sentence; the next one names Helenus, Priam’s son, as the prophet whose forewarnings the Trojans carry away with them.

sentences.t:
Inde futurorum certi, quae cuncta fideli
Priamides Helenus monitu praedixerat, intrant
Sicaniam:
sentences.l: Then, sure of things to come — all of which Helenus, Priam’s son, had foretold in a faithful warning — they enter Sicania:
sentences.i: From there, certain of what was coming — Helenus, Priam’s son, had foretold the whole of it in a warning that held good — they enter Sicania:
sentences.n: certi takes a genitive of the thing one is sure of, and futurorum is a future participle used as a neuter plural noun, “the things that are going to be”. quae cuncta keeps the adjective inside the relative clause: “all which things”, where English wants “all of which”. Priamides is a Greek patronymic in apposition to Helenus. fideli ... monitu is an ablative of means split around the name, fideli closing 722 and monitu standing third in 723.

sentences.t:
tribus haec excurrit in aequora pinnis,
e quibus imbriferos est versa Pachynos ad austros,
mollibus expositum zephyris Lilybaeon, ad arctos
aequoris expertes spectat boreamque Peloros.
sentences.l: this land runs out into the sea with three points, of which Pachynus is turned toward the rain-bringing south winds, Lilybaeum is exposed to the soft west winds, toward the Bears that have no share of the sea and toward Boreas looks Peloros.
sentences.i: Sicily runs out into the sea on three headlands: of them, Pachynus faces the rain-bearing southerlies, Lilybaeum lies open to the soft west winds, and Peloros looks toward the Bears that never touch the sea, and toward the north wind.
sentences.n: Each cape is put differently: est versa, a passive, for Pachynos; then a bare participle, expositum, for Lilybaeon, with est to be supplied; then the active spectat for Peloros, the only one of the three that does the looking itself. pinna is a feather or a fin, so the island runs out into the water on three fins. e quibus is partitive. aequoris expertes is expers with the genitive, “having no share of the sea” — the Bears are the constellations that never set into it. The Greek names keep Greek forms: Pachynos, Lilybaeon, Peloros. Magnus prints tribus ... pinnis; some editions print tribus ... linguis, “with three tongues”.

sentences.t:
Hac subeunt Teucri, et remis aestuque secundo
sub noctem potitur Zanclaea classis harena.
sentences.l: By this way the Teucrians come in, and with oars and a following tide the fleet takes possession of the Zanclean sand toward nightfall.
sentences.i: This is the way the Trojans come in, and with oars and the tide behind them the fleet gains the sand of Zancle as night comes on.
sentences.n: Hac is an ablative of the route taken with via understood — “by this way”, that is, past Peloros, the cape just named. potitur is deponent, active in meaning, and takes the ablative harena. sub noctem is sub with the accusative of time coming on, “towards nightfall”. aestu secundo is the phrase of 630 brought back word for word: the voyage ends on the same following tide it set out on.

sentences.t:
Scylla latus dextrum, laevum inrequieta Charybdis
infestat:
sentences.l: Scylla infests the right side, restless Charybdis the left:
sentences.i: Scylla plagues the right-hand side, restless Charybdis the left:
sentences.n: One singular verb, infestat, serves both subjects and both objects, and it does not arrive until the head of 731. The line is chiastic — Scylla, right side, left, Charybdis — so the two monsters stand outside and the two sides inside. The edition prints inrequieta unassimilated, where the assimilated spelling would be irrequieta; it means never resting, which of a whirlpool is the literal truth.

sentences.t:
vorat haec raptas revomitque carinas,
illa feris atram canibus succingitur alvum,
virginis ora gerens, et, si non omnia vates
ficta reliquerunt aliquo quoque tempore virgo.
sentences.l: this one devours ships she has snatched and vomits them up again, that one is girt about her black belly with savage dogs, wearing a maiden’s face, and — if the poets have not left everything they told as invention — she too was a maiden at some time.
sentences.i: Charybdis swallows the ships she snatches and spews them up again; Scylla is belted round her black belly with savage dogs, and wears a girl’s face — and, if the poets have not left us the whole of it as fiction, she too was a girl once.
sentences.n: haec is the nearer of the two just named and so is Charybdis, illa the further and so Scylla: the pronouns are all that tells them apart, and the idiomatic layer puts the names back. raptas ... carinas encloses revomitque, so the snatching and the spitting out happen inside one phrase. succingitur is passive in form and middle in force, “she girds herself”, with alvum a Greek accusative of respect, “as to her belly” — the construction met at 688. quoque here is the plain adverb “too” and not the quō-que that means “and with which”, though aliquo ... tempore stands round it and invites the mistake. The last clause has no verb — fuit has to be supplied with virgo — and Magnus prints no comma between reliquerunt and aliquo, so the condition runs straight on into what it conditions.

sentences.t: Hanc multi petiere proci;
sentences.l: Many suitors sought her;
sentences.i: Many suitors courted her;
sentences.n: petiere is petierunt, another -ere perfect. petere has been the verb of making for a place all through this part — regia tecta petunt at 638, rura petunt at 720 — and here it is courting a woman: the same word for heading somewhere and for heading after someone.

sentences.t:
quibus illa repulsis
ad pelagi nymphas, pelagi gratissima nymphis,
ibat et elusos iuvenum narrabat amores.
sentences.l: and when they had been driven off she used to go to the nymphs of the sea, most pleasing to the nymphs of the sea, and tell of the cheated loves of young men.
sentences.i: and once she had turned them down she would go to the sea-nymphs — she was the sea-nymphs’ own favourite — and tell them how she had made fools of the young men who loved her.
sentences.n: quibus is a connecting relative, “and when these”, and it stands inside its own ablative absolute, quibus ... repulsis, which English has to open out into a clause. The line between repeats itself: pelagi nymphas after ad, then the same two words again in the dative at the end of 736, pelagi ... nymphis, with gratissima shut inside the second pair. ibat and narrabat are imperfects of habit — this was what she did, over and over. elusos amores are the loves she eluded, the participle passive and the young men left in the genitive.

sentences.t:
Quam, dum pectendos praebet Galatea capillos,
talibus adloquitur, referens suspiria, dictis:
sentences.l: And her, while Galatea offers her hair to be combed, she addresses with words like these, fetching up sighs:
sentences.i: And while Galatea gives her hair to Scylla to comb, she speaks to her with words like these, with sighs coming up between:
sentences.n: Quam is a connecting relative, “and her”, carried over the whole intervening dum-clause to its verb adloquitur, the second word of 739; adloquor is deponent, active in meaning, and takes the accusative. pectendos ... capillos is a gerundive in agreement — hair to be combed — with praebet, which is to offer a thing for something to be done to it. Galatea is the subject of both verbs, so the goddess is the one whose hair is combed and the one who speaks, and Scylla is the Quam, the one doing the combing.

sentences.t:
“Te tamen, o virgo, genus haud inmite virorum
expetit, utque facis, potes his impune negare;
sentences.l: “You, though, o maiden, a race of men not unkind seeks out, and, as you do, you can refuse them without paying for it;
sentences.i: “You, though, girl — the men who want you are no cruel breed, and you can say no to them, as you do, and pay nothing for it;
sentences.n: tamen sets Scylla against the speaker before the speaker has said anything about herself; the contrast is only completed by At mihi at 742. haud inmite is litotes, “not unkind”, which is how Galatea concedes the point. potes ... negare takes the dative of the person refused, his. impune is “without penalty”, and the edition prints inmite with n at 740 and impune with m in the very next line, as it printed inpia with n at 718: the spelling is not levelled even between neighbouring lines.

sentences.t:
At mihi, cui pater est Nereus, quam caerula Doris
enixa est, quae sum turba quoque tuta sororum,
non nisi per luctus licuit Cyclopis amorem
effugere,” —
sentences.l: But for me — whose father is Nereus, whom sea-blue Doris bore, who am safe too in a crowd of sisters — it was not permitted to escape the Cyclops’ love except through griefs,”
sentences.i: But I, whose father is Nereus, whom sea-blue Doris bore, who am safe as well in a crowd of sisters — I was not allowed to escape the Cyclops’ love except by way of grief,”
sentences.n: mihi is the dative with impersonal licuit, “it was permitted to me”, and three relative clauses hang on that one pronoun and pile up her protections — a father, a mother, a crowd of sisters — before the verb says that none of them was enough. cui pater est Nereus is a dative of possession: Latin says “to whom Nereus is a father” where English says “whose father is”. non nisi per luctus is a double negative, “not except through”: the only way out ran through grief, and luctus is accusative plural, griefs one after another. quoque is again the plain adverb. caerula gives the sea’s own colour to a sea-goddess. The dash at the end is the edition’s, and it marks where the speech breaks off.

sentences.t: et lacrimae vocem impediere loquentis.
sentences.l: and tears blocked the voice of her as she spoke.
sentences.i: and tears got in the way of her voice as she spoke.
sentences.n: impediere is impedierunt, an -ere perfect, and the edition spells it with m. loquentis is a present participle in the genitive with no noun to lean on — “of her speaking” — where Latin lets the participle carry the person by itself. The break is mid-line: effugere and the edition’s dash stand at the head of 745, and the tears stop the voice in the second half of the same line.

sentences.t:
Quas ubi marmoreo detersit pollice virgo
et solata deam est, “refer, o carissima,” dixit.
sentences.l: And when the maiden had wiped these away with her marble thumb and had consoled the goddess, “tell it, o dearest,” she said.
sentences.i: And when the girl had wiped them away with her marble-white thumb and had comforted the goddess, “Tell it, dearest,” she said.
sentences.n: Quas is a connecting relative, “and these”, the tears of the line before, and it stands first in its own subordinate clause, ahead of the ubi that introduces the clause — which is where Latin likes to put it and English cannot. solata ... est is the perfect of the deponent solor and is active in meaning. marmoreo pollice is marble for the whiteness and the smoothness of the skin, and the thumb is Scylla’s, since she is the virgo and Galatea is the dea. carissima is a vocative superlative.

sentences.t: “neve tui causam tege (sic sum fida) doloris!”
sentences.l: “and do not hide the cause of your grief (so faithful am I)!”
sentences.i: “and don’t hide what your grief is about — I am that much to be trusted!”
sentences.n: neve carries the imperative refer of the line before on into a prohibition, and tege is a present imperative. tui ... doloris is one genitive phrase pulled to the two ends of the line, tui the second word and doloris the last, with causam, tege and the whole parenthesis between them. The round brackets are the edition’s. And the edition’s punctuation here is worth seeing: it puts a full stop after dixit at the end of 747 and then goes on with the same speech in this line in lower case, so the sentence-point stands at a place where the speech does not stop.

sentences.t: Nereis his contra resecuta Crataeide natam est:
sentences.l: The Nereid in reply to these words answered back the daughter born of Crataeis:
sentences.i: The Nereid answered her back — the daughter Crataeis bore — like this:
sentences.n: resequor takes the accusative of the person answered, so natam is its object: the Nereid answers Scylla, who is named here only as the daughter born of Crataeis. Crataeide is a Greek ablative, and the construction is the ablative of origin with no preposition, as at 692 and 717. contra is adverbial, “back, in return”, with his, “to these words”. resecuta and its auxiliary est have two words pushed between them. Nereis is a Greek nominative and it names Galatea by the father she claimed at 742. The colon at the end opens a speech that lies outside these lines.
